teaser: Turn a flat coffee filter into a tiny canopy and test how air slows its fall.
title: A Coffee Filter Parachute
question: Why does a wide coffee filter parachute float down more slowly than a crumpled filter?
idea: Gravity pulls a parachute down while moving air pushes back; a wide canopy catches more air, creating more drag and slowing the fall.

curiosity.intro: Build one tiny parachute, then change one thing at a time to discover what slows and steadies its fall.
curiosity.carryForward: Watch how the canopy meets the air, and keep every comparison fair.

questions.question: What slows the parachute?
questions.notice: Find the wide canopy above the hanging paperclip and notice the open space it covers.
questions.say: Gravity pulls the parachute down. As it moves, tiny moving pieces of air push back. That air resistance, also called drag, slows the fall; it does not turn gravity off.
questions.try: An adult stays beside you while you attach equal strings or yarn and a paperclip or small toy to a coffee filter. Ask that adult to use the scissors. Drop from standing height, or let the adult hold it higher. Never climb on chairs, stair railings, windows, or balconies.

questions.question: Why does the flat filter fall more slowly?
questions.notice: Compare the open, wide filter with the same kind of filter crumpled into a small shape.
questions.say: The wide filter has more surface area facing the moving air. It catches more air and makes more drag, so it falls more slowly than the crumpled filter even though both filters weigh the same.
questions.try: Drop one filter flat and the same filter crumpled. Count the fall time or use a timer, then open the filter and repeat.

questions.question: What changes when the load is heavier?
questions.notice: Look for one paperclip under one canopy and two paperclips under the matching canopy.
questions.say: With the same canopy, adding a second paperclip gives gravity more weight to pull while the canopy area stays the same. In this test, the heavier parachute usually descends faster. Without air, extra weight would not make an object fall faster.
questions.try: Keep the filter and strings the same. Compare one paperclip with two paperclips over several drops.

questions.question: How can a tiny hole make the fall steadier?
questions.notice: Find the small centered hole and watch the canopy stay open with less side-to-side wobble.
questions.say: A small hole at the canopy top lets some air flow through. That can keep air from spilling unevenly around the edges, so the parachute may wobble less.
questions.try: Predict what a tiny centered hole will change. Test the uncut canopy first, then ask an adult to make the hole and measure several more drops.

reading.title: Six clues in a slow fall
reading.coverText: Follow gravity down and feel the air push back.
reading.parentNote: Grade 3 reading. Welcome spoken answers, pointing, drawing, and dictation; the scenic plates show the test ideas rather than exact measurements.
reading.foldableTitle: A little book of parachute clues
reading.foldableNote: Carry six slow-fall clues in a small book.

beats.title: Two pulls in one fall
beats.passage: Big held the coffee filter open like a tiny canopy. Gravity pulled the parachute toward the floor. As it moved, tiny moving pieces of air pushed back. This air resistance, or drag, slowed the fall but did not stop gravity.
beats.prompt: Which two forces act in different directions during the fall?

foldable.heading: Gravity and drag
foldable.body: Gravity pulls the parachute down. Moving air pushes back with air resistance, or drag, slowing the fall without stopping gravity.

beats.title: Wide meets more air
beats.passage: Little dropped the filter flat, then crumpled the same filter and dropped it again. Its weight had not changed, but its shape had. The wide filter showed more surface area to the air, made more drag, and floated down longer.
beats.prompt: Why is shape—not weight—the best explanation for this result?

foldable.heading: Wide meets air
foldable.body: The flat filter and crumpled filter weigh the same. The wide shape meets more air, makes more drag, and falls more slowly.

beats.title: A heavier load
beats.passage: Next they kept the canopy and strings the same. One parachute carried one paperclip; another carried two. The extra weight made that parachute descend faster in air. This does not mean heavier things always fall faster: without air, there would be no drag.
beats.prompt: What stayed the same, and what changed in the paperclip test?

foldable.heading: Change the weight
foldable.body: With the same canopy and strings, two paperclips add weight. In air, that parachute usually reaches the floor sooner.

beats.title: A fair test
beats.passage: Big suggested a fair test: change one thing at a time. They predicted a bigger canopy would fall more slowly, then kept the weight and string length equal. They measured several drops because one wobbly fall could fool them.
beats.prompt: Why did they keep the weight and strings equal and repeat each drop?

foldable.heading: A fair test
foldable.body: Change one thing at a time, keep the others equal, and measure several drops. Repeating helps a result become more trustworthy.

beats.title: A tiny steadying hole
beats.passage: Sometimes the canopy rocked from side to side as air spilled unevenly around its rim. A small hole at the top let a little air pass through. The parachute wobbled less, so its path became steadier.
beats.prompt: How can letting some air through reduce wobble?

foldable.heading: A steadier fall
foldable.body: A tiny hole at the canopy top lets some air through. The flow can become more even, so the parachute wobbles less.

beats.title: From filters to landers
beats.passage: Their paper parachute was small, but its mechanism was real. Parachutes for people and space landers also spread a large canopy through air. Gravity keeps pulling down while drag pushes against motion, helping the load land more slowly.
beats.prompt: What big idea do the model, a human parachute, and a lander parachute share?

foldable.heading: The same big idea
foldable.body: Human and space-lander parachutes use wide canopies too. Gravity pulls down while drag pushes against motion and slows the descent.

math.title: Compare and round parachute measures
math.intro: Compare test notes, then round measurements to the nearest ten.

tasks.prompt: Across several drops, a flat filter floats for 42 counted seconds in all and a crumpled filter for 28. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater total?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. Write the symbol, then give the greater total.
tasks.worked: 42 > 28. Four tens are more than two tens, so the greater total is 42 seconds.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: One set of parachute strings is 76 centimeters long and another is 67 centimeters. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the greater length?
tasks.hint: Compare tens first, then ones. Write the symbol, then give the greater length.
tasks.worked: 76 > 67. Seven tens are more than six tens, so the greater length is 76 centimeters.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: Big and Little each record 48 test drops. Put >, <, or = in the circle. What is the shared number when the totals are equal?
tasks.hint: Compare tens and ones. When both totals match, use = and give that shared number.
tasks.worked: 48 = 48. Both totals match, so the shared number is 48 drops.
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: The supply box holds 23 paperclips. What is 23 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones digit. With 4 or less, round down to the ten before.
tasks.worked: 23 has 3 ones, so round down to 20 paperclips.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: A piece of string is 57 centimeters long. What is 57 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: Look at the ones digit. With 5 or more, round up to the next ten.
tasks.worked: 57 has 7 ones, so round up to 60 centimeters.
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: A safe standing-height drop is measured as 95 centimeters. What is 95 rounded to the nearest ten?
tasks.hint: A ones digit of 5 rounds up to the next ten.
tasks.worked: 95 has 5 ones, so round up to 100 centimeters.
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Choose one two-digit measurement from a new drop test. Compare it with another result, then round it to the nearest ten.
math.printNote: Write one answer in each blank. For comparisons, also put >, <, or = in the circle.
math.parentNote: Grade 2 math. Six tasks compare two-digit values or round a two-digit value to the nearest ten.
math.answerKeyIntro: Grade 2 math. Compare tens before ones; for rounding, 5 or more rounds up and 4 or less rounds down.

quiz.title: Four parachute clues
quiz.intro: Follow gravity, drag, weight, and a steadier fall.

questions.prompt: What does air resistance do to a falling parachute?
choices: It pushes against the motion and slows the fall
It pulls the load toward the floor
questions.answer: Air resistance, or drag, pushes against the parachute's motion and slows its fall.

questions.prompt: Why does a flat coffee filter usually fall more slowly than the same filter crumpled?
choices: Its wide surface meets more air
questions.answer: The wide filter shows more surface area to the air, creating more drag while its weight stays the same.

questions.prompt: Which plan makes a fair canopy-size test?
choices: Change canopy size but keep weight and strings equal
Change canopy, weight, and strings together
questions.answer: Change only canopy size, keep weight and strings equal, and repeat the drops.

questions.prompt: What can a tiny centered hole at the canopy top do?
choices: Let some air through and reduce wobble
Make the canopy catch every bit of air
questions.answer: A tiny top hole can let some air through more evenly, which may reduce wobble.

parentGuidance: Gravity pulls a parachute down while air resistance, or drag, pushes against its motion. A wide canopy creates more drag; weight, canopy area, shape, release, and air currents can all affect a test, so change one thing at a time and repeat drops. Stay beside the child, use scissors only with grown-up help, and drop only from standing height or from a grown-up's raised hand—never climb on chairs, stair railings, windows, or balconies. Keep paperclips and small toys away from mouths.
